findings.summary: The round-2 fix only applies 'tell the CRM only what reached Redis' to the handover_changed event. crm_send.send still reports a takeover that reached memory only in its synchronous 200 answer (handover.active=true), and the CRM stores that answer first. Since 38556e7 that answer also has no matching event, which breaks contract R3 ('one value from both').
findings.failure: The visitor store has a stalled Redis, so its SET raises redis TimeoutError (or any one failure has started the 30 s offline window). The idempotency key is on crm_send's own Redis client, which has no breaker, so it still works. The CRM agent sends a reply to a visitor who is not held. Meta accepts. _take_over -> handover.begin -> user_store.save falls back to memory, and _tell_crm now logs 'changed in memory only ... not telling the CRM' and queues nothing. _take_over still returns {active: true, expires_at: now+HANDOVER_IDLE_SECONDS, occurred_at}, and send answers 200 with it. The CRM stores wa_handover_active=true and the expiry. Redis was never written, so after the window the bot reads 'not held' and answers the visitor over the agent, while the CRM shows the agent holding the conversation until expires_at (24 h once 42.2 lands). This is the harm the new _tell_crm docstring describes ('leaves it showing a state the bot will not be in, with no error anywhere to retry'), reached through the other channel. The touch branch has the same flaw: a renewal that reached memory only is answered with a pushed-out expires_at that Redis does not have. Not a regression in what the CRM ends up believing: before 38556e7, the event and the response both said active. But the commit claims the rule covers starting and renewing ('Same rule for starting and renewing a takeover'), and for send the rule is half-applied. The response now disagrees with the event stream.

findings.summary: _tell_crm uses user_store.offline(), which is process-wide and based on time, as a stand-in for 'this save reached Redis'. Another thread's failure that lands between this save's successful SET and the check makes a change that did reach Redis go untold, and nothing ever re-sends it.
findings.failure: Thread A: begin/end/touch -> SET succeeds -> (thread B's read times out and calls _go_offline) -> A's _tell_crm sees offline() True -> no event. Redis has the new state and the CRM never hears of it. For a console takeover or console hand-back, the CRM stays wrong until the next change. The window is a few bytecodes wide, but on a Redis that is going bad (when B's 1 s timeout is most likely) it is not zero. A save that returned whether it reached Redis would make this exact. I only read the code for this one and did not try to reproduce it.

self_check.spec_coverage: The round-2 repro scenario (SET of the ended record fails, so no active=false event beside the 503) is now covered by the existing save-failure test with an added assertion on the queue. I confirmed that test reads the real crm_events queue fixture, so it is not a tautology. The new test covers begin with a failed save. No test covers crm_send.send's answer when its begin/touch save fails, and that answer is the CRM's main channel. That is P2-1, red in the repro. Without Redis, offline() is always False, so the 40.2/41.3 behaviour is unchanged on the memory-only path, which is the one the existing suite uses.
self_check.e2e: Not run end to end. /internal/crm/* is only reachable on the shared Docker network, and I did not touch the production chatbot or the CRM. That the CRM stores the synchronous send answer first comes from the 41.3 contract text the developer cites ('the CRM gets one value from both', the event 'fills in the CRM's copy if this answer never reaches it'). I did not exercise it against acuven_crm_demo. The repro drives the real FastAPI route, real user_store with redis' own TimeoutError on SET, real crm_events.enqueue, and real whatsapp.send_raw stubbed one layer down at httpx.post.
self_check.security: Nothing new. No new endpoint, secret or logged personal data. The new ERROR line logs key_id, which is the full phone number (or BSUID). The existing handover INFO lines already log key_id in full, so this is not a new exposure. AR-1/AR-2 are unaffected.

The one unjustified gap is that the stated rule ('same rule for starting and renewing a takeover') is applied to the event and not to send's response, which tells the CRM the same thing (P2-1).

phase2.rebuttals: Process note first: the developer's round-2 entry in todo.md came back in the same command as my `git status` check, before findings.json was written. By then P2-1's repro had already been written and run red and P3-1 had already been identified, so neither came from reading the entry. Now the arguments. 1) Does not hold: '规则是「只告诉 CRM 真正写进 Redis 的状态」，开始 / 续期 / 结束都适用'. It applies to one of the two channels. crm_send.send answers the CRM with _take_over's crm_state whether or not the save reached Redis, so a memory-only begin/touch is still told to the CRM, just not by event (P2-1, red). 2) Partly does not hold: '没配 Redis 时 offline() 恒为假，40.2 / 41.3 的行为与测试不变'. That is true without Redis. With Redis configured and offline, 41.3's send changes behaviour: it used to give a response and an event that agreed, and now gives a response with a takeover and no event. That breaks the R3 promise the code itself cites in _take_over ('the CRM gets one value from both'). 3) Holds: keeping both 503 checks in hand_back. The second one is now also what keeps a partly failed multi-record hand-back honest. 4) Holds, though it is a judgement call: leaving the console TOOL_END. For those 30 s, memory is what the bot acts on. 5) Holds: the mutation (remove the check -> 3 failed) shows the new test and the round-2 repro both depend on the check.
phase2.blind_spot: The developer lists the get()/_offline_until boundary race as a known, unfixed microsecond window. I did not look at that one. I looked at a mirror race instead (a successful SET followed by another thread tripping offline, P3-1), and only by reading the code. Both come from the same design choice: a global breaker read after the fact as a stand-in for 'did this one call reach Redis'. I reported one face of it and missed the other, which shows I followed the write path and not the read side of the same flag. The developer's other admissions (the round-2 test never asserted on the queue, the read-modify-save race since task 20, the round limit reached) are either process notes or out of scope. The concrete thing they did not see is P2-1. It has the same shape as last round: a rule stated in their own words ('same rule for starting and renewing') and a second channel the rule does not reach.
